title: In the AI era, the most valuable thing isn't intelligence, it's the audit trail
dek: Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever lays the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.
why: Worth listening to for vertical AI founders, investment banking/PE practitioners, and enterprise software investors. The first half's product history is average in information density; the second half's pricing, audit, and sales mechanics are more valuable.
who: Vertical AI founders, investment banking and PE practitioners, and investors looking at enterprise software and the AI application layer. For anyone who wants to know how to build that layer of plumbing beyond the model, how to price it, and how to sell it into large institutions.
skip: The product-era retrospective from 1:24 to 6:14 at the start is mostly setup; you can fast-forward to the mechanics section after 16:57.

points.h: Model companies are refineries, vertical companies are chemical plants
points.body: Gabe reasons from Dario's line: if tomorrow a whole data center full of geniuses appeared at the door of Goldman, Millennium, Citadel, these institutions would still take a long time to figure out how to change the way they work and how to wire it into their systems. So he thinks the biggest challenge for every great investor over the next five years is not getting access to intelligence, but wiring AI into the investment lifecycle. This also explains why he isn't worried about Anthropic and OpenAI: finance is a collection of niches with different data, definitions, and regulatory requirements, and for Anthropic to stop and pick up this coin would be like pulling over on the road from $100 billion in revenue to $1 trillion.

points.h: Applied AI companies have a first-mover disadvantage
points.body: Gabe says companies that did applied AI early were actually at a disadvantage: you think you know where the world is going, you build the product for that end state, but the model isn't there yet, and after users try it they just say ‘this is garbage.’ Rogo went through this phase itself. His judgment is that if your read on the end state is right and you keep building toward it, the moment the model catches up is the magic moment. He ties Rogo's product eras directly to model eras: 01 Pro was the first version reliable enough to at least serve as a search tool; by Opus 4.5, and from late 2025 into early 2026, the model can basically do anything a junior investment or banking professional does, provided you give it the right instructions and context.

points.h: The MD annotating on an iPad is the real last mile
points.body: Gabe gives an example as concrete as it gets: the typical workflow of an investment banking MD is to email deck comments to an analyst, and Rogo lets that MD email the comments to an AI analyst, get back a revised draft in 20 minutes instead of two days, automatically notify the junior analysts on the deal, and show a full audit trail of every small change. He points out the key: this finance professional hasn't logged into a computer in ten years, but he has an iPad, and he knows how to annotate on an iPad. This kind of product detail for a specific end user can only be built by someone with a ‘spidey sense’ for the job.

points.h: The harness matters more than the model itself
points.body: Gabe uses Claude Code and Claude Cowork versus ChatGPT as an example: the models are actually similar, but Claude's harness and presentation are much better, letting the model exercise more long-horizon capabilities, and so usage and expansion took off. He extends the analogy to the brain: humans have high agency not just because of raw memory, IQ, and knowledge, but because there are a bunch of microservices in the head — how to store knowledge, how to retrieve it, how to trigger it, and emotion is one way of triggering a microservice. A great investor's judgment comes from seeing something in the market that triggers a memory of some event, leading to a creative decision. These microservices are what vertical companies need to build.

points.h: From per-seat pricing, jump straight to outcome-based pricing
points.body: Rogo today is classic enterprise software: priced per seat, because buyers are used to comparing it to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, PitchBook, and every deal signed requires an AE plus a solutions architect to shake hands and explain the integration. Gabe says Anthropic can sell to them easily, with spend rising exponentially and no human involvement, because it's a token-consumption model; but many industries can't ride the token-consumption wave, and Rogo is one of them, so it has to build its GTM machine at five times the speed. His pricing judgment is that every enterprise will go through two pricing revolutions: first to usage based, then to outcome based. He'd rather skip tokens and usage and ask clients directly: how much do you charge per good investment idea? How much per quarterly LP report? How much per investment banking CIM?

Gabe says accuracy is of course still super important, but auditability matters more than accuracy, and the two are often conflated. The logic: if the answer is inaccurate and you don't know how to check it or see where it came from, then whether it's accurate or not you can't use it, because you don't trust it. Conversely, if it's right most of the time, and even when it's wrong you can clearly see the assumptions and data sources, it's still actionable and still saves time. As tools move from copilot to autopilot — not just retrieving information, but having agency, actually making investment decisions or sending emails — you have to be able to look back at why it decided the way it did, because you need to debug it, just as when an individual investor makes a bad decision you check whether the data input was wrong or someone lied to him. In regulated capital markets, if you can't explain the basis for a decision, you simply can't get it past the line.

points.h: The company brain is called Shrek, and all conversations are recorded
points.body: All conversations inside Rogo are recorded, and new hires are told on day one ‘you are always being recorded,’ and this content is filtered into the company brain, named Shrek because the engineers thought that was funny. There's a dashboard that shows the ‘swamp’ of what everyone is doing, connected to the company's various systems, with a very clear sense of company goals, values, what needs to be delivered to clients, and the north star metric, so it can shape every answer and deliverable. It's both passive and active: you can go in and ask ‘how should I pitch the value proposition and savings of model routing to a large institution,’ and it pulls the information out; it also proactively reminds you ‘Patrick, I see you're meeting this private credit firm on Thursday, here's what you should know, the use cases that will resonate, and the ROI metrics companies you've worked with in the past want to hear.’ Gabe says this is the core problem of enablement: suck information in, and give it out when people need it.

points.h: What it's like to be rejected by 40 investors in a row
points.body: Gabe says the hardest low point was the A round: at the time there were no star investors on the cap table, David Tisch introduced him to 40 investors, he met Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark and so on, and all 40 passed. And it wasn't the send-a-deck-no-interest kind, it was ‘interesting, meet Gabe’‘like Gabe, chat for an hour’‘come to IC’‘let's have a meal’‘come by again on the weekend’ — and then ‘we've decided not to invest.’ He says that phase had nothing to do with anything, only with you, like being dumped by 40 girlfriends, each time you fell in love, each time the other person said it's not for you. In the end Thrive didn't invest either; Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone had passed, and Gabe asked Keith back: if this isn't a contrarian bet, why do all your friends say it's a bad idea and don't believe in me? He sums up three reasons investors didn't invest: underestimating the finance TAM, the product genuinely being bad at the time, and not having enough data points to believe he could chew glass and ship the next version.

points.h: Finance meets the innovator's dilemma for the first time
points.body: Gabe says that over the past 10 to 20 years, capital allocation and investing have been very profitable businesses, extremely hard to enter, especially in private markets, raise one fund then raise another, the business has its own inertia, and it's hard to screw up. So for a long time there was no market shock that made every investment firm and every bank say ‘I have to completely rethink what I'm doing.’ Now there is: hundreds of AI-native disruptors, AI-native investment firms, AI-native investment banks will emerge to attack existing business models. He defines AI-native as willing to constantly reinvent everything, addicted to AI to the point of not caring what looks completely unrealistic, just moving in the direction of integrating this alien foundational technology into everything, with no part of the business sacred.

terms.def: The layer of engineering that wraps the model and determines how it is invoked and presented, affecting the experience more than the model itself.
Material Non-Public Information, the most compliance-sensitive category of information at investment banks and investment firms.
The core document an investment firm submits to its investment committee to argue for a deal.
Due Diligence Questionnaire, a long list of standard questions sent by the other side in a deal or fundraising.
Confidential Information Memorandum, the core pitch document an investment bank shows potential buyers when selling a company.
The ability to let an agent compress memory into limited tokens during a long conversation without losing key context.
